power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .051", "p = .22"), Sentence = c("M = -0.04, SD = 0.71; t(1130.24) = 1.96, p = .051, d = 0.12, 95%-CI [-0.00, 0.23]).", "The overall pattern of correlations in Table 3 did not differ significantly between boys and girls (Steiger's omnibus test: χ² = 65.19, permutation p = .22)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

This study suggests that children's interests already show gender-related patterns in third grade: boys, on average, showed stronger interests in thing-oriented activities, whereas girls showed stronger interests in people-and idea-oriented activities.

These patterns were visible beyond school subjects, and the People-Things difference changed little over six months, suggesting that gendered interest development may begin before students make educational or career choices.

The findings indicate that educators and researchers may benefit from paying attention to broad activity preferences, not only subject-specific interests, when trying to understand children's developing motivation.
A central developmental question concerns when interests become systematically organized, how stable such patterns are, and whether they already differ by gender in childhood.

From early childhood onward, interests guide which activities children seek out, persist in, and avoid; thereby shaping not only what children engage with but also how they learn from these experiences.

These selective engagements accumulate over time, shaping learning experiences in elementary school and laying foundations for later educational and career pathways (Ainley, 2006; Elsworth et al., 1999; Krapp, 2007; Nye et al., 2017; Schiefele et al., 1993).

text.text: In learning contexts, interest is associated with sustained attention (Ainley, 2006; Hidi & Renninger, 2006), a greater willingness to invest effort (Ainley et al., 2002; Hidi & Renninger, 2006), and deeper processing (e.g., Schiefele, 1990), all of which can support comprehension and meaningful skill acquisition.

text.text: Such processes may become particularly visible in elementary school, where children encounter a broader range of structured and self-chosen activities.
Repeated engagement can consolidate into relatively stable preferences that become part of children's developing selfunderstanding and identity (Hidi & Renninger, 2006; Krapp, 2007; Renninger, 1992).

text.text: If enduring patterns of engagement begin to take shape already in elementary school, examining interests this early becomes relevant for understanding how motivational orientations connect to knowledge acquisition and emerging competence differences (Lechner et al., 2019).

text.text: Importantly, interest is not a unitary construct.

Rather, educational research distinguishes more situational states of interest from more enduring individual traits and emphasizes that interest is tied to specific objects, activities, and domains (Hidi & Renninger, 2006; Renninger & Hidi, 2011).
text.formatted: Rather, educational research distinguishes more situational states of interest from more enduring individual traits and emphasizes that interest is tied to specific objects, activities, and domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hidi & Renninger, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Renninger & Hidi, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Interest development in childhood is therefore not only about overall engagement, but also about how preferences become organized across activities and domains.
One prominent source of such organization is gender, which has been shown to structure interests and preferences later in development and may already do so in childhood (Jacobs et al., 2002).
text.formatted: One prominent source of such organization is gender, which has been shown to structure interests and preferences later in development and may already do so in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Jacobs et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the present study examines whether gender-related interest patterns are already observable among third graders (mean age = 8.62 years), using a newly developed RIASEC-based self-report measure of broad activity preferences.
The measure assesses preferences for concrete activities, such as building a tree house or caring for other children, rather than interest in school subjects such as mathematics or German.
We also examine how these preferences relate to subject-specific academic interests and school grades.

Research on interest has developed along two mainly separate traditions: an educational-psychological tradition focused on interest in school domains and learning contexts, and a vocational-psychological tradition focused on broader activity preferences and interest profiles.
Both perspectives are relevant in elementary school, where children's interests may be organized both within curricular domains and across activities that cut across school subjects.

In the more educational-psychological tradition, interest is typically conceptualized as a domain-or subject-specific construct tied to school-related content and activities, such as mathematics, language, or science (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020; Jansen et al., 2016; Köller et al., 2001; Renninger & Hidi, 2011; Tröbst et al., 2016).

text.text: This line of research focuses on how interests develop through instructional experiences, how they support engagement and achievement, and how they can be fostered through educational interventions (e.g., Hübner et al., 2017).

text.text: Consistent with this focus, interest is typically associated with achievement, especially when measured with appropriate specificity, although effect sizes are usually modest (Schiefele et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Consistent with this focus, interest is typically associated with achievement, especially when measured with appropriate specificity, although effect sizes are usually modest <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Schiefele et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Situated expectancy-value theory provides a useful framework for this tradition because it conceptualizes children's engagement and choices as shaped by their expectancies for success and by the subjective value they attach to specific tasks, activities, and domains, including intrinsic value or interest (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024).

text.text: This tradition also aligns with research on academic self-concept, which conceptualizes children's self-beliefs as multidimensional and increasingly differentiated by school subject as domain-specific experiences and feedback accumulate (Arens et al., 2021; Marsh, 1990; Möller, 2024; Shavelson et al., 1976).

text.text: From this perspective, subject-specific interests, value and expectancy beliefs, and self-beliefs are expected to co-develop, reflecting how children evaluate and value their experiences in particular domains (Denissen et al., 2007; Eccles & Wigfield, 2024).
text.formatted: From this perspective, subject-specific interests, value and expectancy beliefs, and self-beliefs are expected to co-develop, reflecting how children evaluate and value their experiences in particular domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Denissen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Eccles & Wigfield, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, vocational psychology typically conceptualizes interests as relatively stable, trait-like preferences for activities that help individuals select and function well in environments that match their orientations, often framed in terms of person-environment fit (Hoff et al., 2020; Holland, 1997).
text.formatted: In contrast, vocational psychology typically conceptualizes interests as relatively stable, trait-like preferences for activities that help individuals select and function well in environments that match their orientations, often framed in terms of person-environment fit <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Hoff et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Holland, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: The most influential structural representation within this tradition is Holland's RIASEC model, which distinguishes six interest domains-Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional-and assumes that these domains form a systematic circumplex configuration, such that adjacent domains are more similar whereas opposing domains are more dissimilar (Holland, 1997; Prediger, 1982).

text.text: This circumplex space is commonly summarized by two orthogonal core dimensions, People versus Things and Data versus Ideas (Lippa, 1998; Prediger, 1982; Su et al., 2009), and recent latent-variable work supports its internal and external validity, including its links to constructs such as self-concepts (Etzel et al., 2021).

text.text: Beyond its structural properties, longitudinal and meta-analytic evidence indicates that interest fit predicts satisfaction and career success indicators over time, and that vocational interests are related to consequential later outcomes (Hanna et al., 2021; Hoff et al., 2020; Stoll et al., 2017), and that RIASEC profiles become increasingly differentiated and stable as students approach educational and occupational decisions (Tracey, 2002; Tracey et al., 2006).

text.text: The two traditions are complementary in elementary school, where children's engagement extends well beyond formal instruction.

From a RIASEC-model perspective, children more broadly engage in activities such as building and tinkering (Realistic), exploring and experimenting (Investigative), drawing and performing (Artistic), helping and caring (Social), persuading and leading (Enterprising), and sorting and organizing (Conventional).
Such activities cut across school subjects and occur in multiple contexts, including classrooms, homes, sports clubs, and settings of extracurricular enrichment.
Despite not being tied to specific curricular domains, they are consequential for educational outcomes because they afford repeated practice and skill development.

Thus, they provide opportunities for knowledge acquisition in line with investment accounts that describe how general capacities such as fluid intelligence are translated into domain-specific competencies over time (Cattell, 1987; Cunha & Heckman, 2007).
text.formatted: Thus, they provide opportunities for knowledge acquisition in line with investment accounts that describe how general capacities such as fluid intelligence are translated into domain-specific competencies over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cattell, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cunha & Heckman, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: A RIASEC-based perspective is therefore well placed to describe children's broader activity preferences as a structured map of what they are repeatedly drawn to, and can complement educational research that views interest as becoming increasingly subject-specific with growing domain experience (Gogol et al., 2016; Weich et al., 2024) by capturing activity-based preferences that show meaningful links to learning outcomes (Höft & Bernholt, 2021).

text.text: However, whether elementary-school children already show a coherent organization of such broader activity preferences and how it should be measured remains an open question.

Although standardized measurement tools are largely lacking in childhood, evidence suggests that vocationally flavored interests can be meaningfully assessed through age-appropriate activity descriptions (Pässler & Hell, 2020; Pässler & Schneider, 2018; Tracey & Ward, 1998).

text.text: For example, younger children may respond more reliably to concrete activity descriptions than to abstract occupational labels (Tracey & Caulum, 2015; Tracey & Ward, 1998).

text.text: Consistent with this, studies using the Inventory of Children's Activities show that younger children's evaluations of activities are often organized around concrete and socially salient features, including gender-typed meanings and situational context (Tracey & Ward, 1998).

text.text: More generally, research on vocational interests in childhood rarely includes samples below the age of ten or prior to fourth grade (Pässler & Hell, 2020; Phipps, 1995; Rohlfing et al., 2012).

text.text: Consequently, evidence on the structural organization of vocational-like interests before late elementary school remains limited, leaving open when a RIASEC-like circumplex begins to develop.
Understanding how interests become structured in childhood is particularly important for explaining gendered educational pathways.

In educational psychology, gender differences are most consistently discussed with respect to subject-specific motivation (e.g., interest, intrinsic value), self-concept, and participation, especially in STEM domains (Ganley & Lubienski, 2016; Jacobs et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In educational psychology, gender differences are most consistently discussed with respect to subject-specific motivation (e.g., interest, intrinsic value), self-concept, and participation, especially in STEM domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ganley & Lubienski, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Jacobs et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Wang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Empirically, a recurring pattern is that gender differences in motivational variables can be noticeable even when gender differences in achievement are comparatively small (e.g., Sewasew et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Empirically, a recurring pattern is that gender differences in motivational variables can be noticeable even when gender differences in achievement are comparatively small (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Sewasew et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This divergence matters because motivational beliefs are robust predictors of later engagement and educational choices (e.g., elective course taking), above and beyond prior performance (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Marsh et al., 2005).
text.formatted: This divergence matters because motivational beliefs are robust predictors of later engagement and educational choices (e.g., elective course taking), above and beyond prior performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Marsh et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, gendered motivational patterns are not uniform across broad labels such as "STEM".

Recent work suggests that stereotypes, perceived fit, and interest can vary substantially across specific STEM fields, implying that early interest development may already be differentiated at a finer-grained level than typical STEM versus non-STEM distinctions (Master et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work suggests that stereotypes, perceived fit, and interest can vary substantially across specific STEM fields, implying that early interest development may already be differentiated at a finer-grained level than typical STEM versus non-STEM distinctions <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Master et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the educational-psychological literature commonly reports a stereotypical configuration, with girls tending to show higher motivation in language-related domains and boys tending to show higher motivation in science-related domains (Lv et al., 2022; Yeung et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Overall, the educational-psychological literature commonly reports a stereotypical configuration, with girls tending to show higher motivation in language-related domains and boys tending to show higher motivation in science-related domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Lv et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Yeung et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These early differences are not typically viewed as purely inherent preferences, but also as motivational outcomes that may be shaped by socialization and meanings attached to domains and activities.

For example, expectancy value perspectives emphasize that children's interests develop from what they think they can do (expectancies) and what they perceive as valuable or fitting for them (values), and both components are sensitive to cues from parents, teachers, peers, and broader cultural stereotypes (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020 , 2024; Jacobs et al., 2002).

text.text: Gender role expectations can influence which activities are encouraged, modeled, and socially rewarded, thereby affecting children's opportunities for practice and the feedback they receive.
Importantly, such influences can operate very early.

For example, teachers' traditional gender role attitudes have been shown to undermine boys' reading-related motivation and skills already in preschool, illustrating that gendered beliefs in the environment can translate into differential motivational development long before children make formal educational choices (Wolter et al., 2015).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that gendered interest patterns may emerge through repeated, cumulative experiences in which activities become associated with gender-typed meanings.
In the vocational tradition, gender differences regarding interests in older samples are often summarized by the People versus Things dimension.
Meta-analytic evidence shows robust differences, with men tending to report higher Realistic interests and women tending to report higher Social interests (Su et al., 2009).

text.text: Longitudinal findings further suggest that these differences are already detectable by late childhood (Hoff et al., 2018; Pässler & Hell, 2020), with girls' vocational interest profiles being more clearly differentiated across domains than boys' (Fouad & Mohler, 2004; Xu & Tracey, 2016).

text.text: Recent research in Brazil also found higher Realistic interests among boys and higher Artistic and Social interests among girls (De Fruyt et al., 2025).

text.text: This extends the evidence beyond European and North American samples, although the Brazilian participants were adolescents and thus older than the third graders studied here.
At the same time, the development of a coherent circumplex structure remains elusive.

Early work suggests that younger children's preferences may be organized around familiarity and enjoyment ("fun" activities), situational and contextual features (where and with whom an activity occurs), and socially salient meanings, including gender stereotypes, rather than around abstract dimensions such as the People-Things and Data-Ideas axes (Tracey & Ward, 1998).

text.text: In this age range, preferences may therefore remain comparatively concrete and anchored in observable activity features and contexts, which could limit the emergence of broad-dimensional profile differences such as People-Things.
Consequently, gender differences that are robust on the People-Things dimension in adolescence and adulthood may be attenuated or not yet detectable in elementary school.
Longitudinal work in older samples supports the idea that structural coherence increases across adolescence (Tracey, 2002; Tracey et al., 2006).

text.text: However, the question remains at what age a circumplex structure begins to take shape.
Research on vocational-like-or activity-based-interests in young children is still limited and measurement instruments for this age group are scarce.
In the present study, we examine whether gender-related interest patterns are already observable in third grade and how they relate to subject-specific academic interests and school grades.

Because no comprehensive RIASEC-based self-report measure exists for children of this age, we developed an age-appropriate instrument that captures the six RIASEC domains through concrete activity descriptions suitable for children at this age, with the goal of representing broad activity preferences without relying on abstract occupational titles.
Third graders were assessed at two time points approximately six months apart.
We addressed four research aims.
First, in developing a new self-report instrument for elementary school children, we examined the fit of children's interest profiles to a RIASEC-like circumplex.
We selected a short form using T1 data and evaluated its circumplex fit at T2 for temporal cross-validation.
Second, we examined gender differences in interest profiles.

Based on previous findings in older samples, we expected emerging gender-typed patterns aligned with the People versus Things dimension, with boys showing relatively stronger things-oriented interests and girls showing relatively stronger people-oriented interests (Pässler & Hell, 2020; Su et al., 2009).

text.text: However, we also considered the alternative possibility that such broad-dimensional differences are weak or absent at this age, because primary-school children's activity preferences may still be relatively concrete and contextbound rather than organized along abstract People-Things and Data-Ideas orientations.
Accordingly, in addition to mean differences in the six interest domains, we examined gender differences in profile orientations along the broader People-Things and Data-Ideas dimensions.
Third, we investigated stability of the assessed interests over approximately six months.
Specifically, we examined mean-level change in profile coordinates and rank-order stability of the six domain scores over this period.
Fourth, we studied the relationship of interests with academic and subject-specific interests, and school grades.
The research objectives of the present study were not preregistered.

text.text: Building on Holland's (1997) RIASEC model and established interest measures for adolescents and adults (e.g., Bergmann & Eder, 1992; Tracey & Ward, 1998), we newly developed an age-appropriate self-report inventory to assess Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, and Conventional interests.

text.text: Each domain was measured with seven items, totaling 42 items.
Items were presented to students by providing them with the stem "How much are you interested in …?", followed by specific activity statements.
Responses were given on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much).

Example items include "building a tree house" (Realistic), "mixing liquids" (Investigative), "drawing pictures" (Artistic), "listening to other children's problems" (Social), "selling something to others" (Enterprising), and "sorting things" (Conventional).

The full questionnaire (German original and English translation of items), including descriptive statistics for each item for both measurement points, can be found in the supplementary materials (SM Table 1).

text.text: Students' academic interests in core school domains were assessed via self-reports at both measurement points.

Children indicated how much they liked school-related activities in German (reading, writing, dictation), mathematics (mental arithmetic, written arithmetic, word problems), cultural/science-related topics (e.g., learning about the local environment, arts-and-crafts/creative activities, learning about nature), and foreign languages (e.g., speaking, writing, and learning vocabulary in English or French).
Items were answered on the same 5-point response scale as the RIASEC-like interest inventory.
For each domain, responses were aggregated to form mean scale scores.

In the present subsample, academic-interest data were available for n = 1,070 students at T1 and for n = 854 students at T2; missingness was negligible among those with available data (0.4% partially missing at T1; 0% at T2).
All items (German original and English translation), including descriptive statistics for each item for both measurement points, can be found in the supplementary materials (SM Table 2).

Information was obtained from the participating schools via teachers.
For the present analyses, we used midterm grades (T2), ranging from 1 (very good) to 6 (insufficient).
Grades at the end of elementary school are highly consequential in the German school system, as they inform promotion decisions and the transition to secondary education tracks.
Grade information was available for n = 995 students (0.2% partially missing).

text.text: The SSM fitted a cosine curve to the six mean domain scores at the theoretical angular positions (R = 0°, I = 60°, A = 120°, S = 180°, E = 240°, C = 300°).

We estimated elevation, representing the mean interest level across domains; amplitude, indicating the degree of profile differentiation; and angular displacement, denoting the peak orientation of the profile within the RIASEC space.
Model fit was assessed using R², with values above .80 indicating good fit to the cosine function and values above .70 considered adequate (Wright et al., 2009).

text.text: The SSM used complete sets of the six domain scores separately at each wave; children were not required to have complete profiles at both waves.
The original 42-item questionnaire was developed on theoretical grounds to represent the six RIASEC domains through age-appropriate activity descriptions.

Because the present study was the first administration of the newly developed instrument, the initial item pool was subject to empirical evaluation and refinement, an integral step in the iterative process of questionnaire development (Clark & Watson, 2019).

text.text: The full questionnaire showed limited circumplex fit, particularly for boys.
We therefore decided to construct a short form with satisfactory circumplex fit for both boys and girls while retaining representation of all six theoretically defined domains.
This decision was made post hoc and was not preregistered.
As a positive side effect, a shorter questionnaire may also reduce response burden in future applications with young children.

To identify a suitable item combination, we applied Ant Colony Optimization (ACO; Olaru et al., 2019; Schroeders et al., 2016), a metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of ants.

text.text: Each artificial ant constructs a candidate item set, and items from better-performing sets become more likely to be selected in subsequent iterations, much as pheromone trails guide ants toward shorter routes.
The optimization procedure selected four of the original seven items per domain by maximizing the lower of the two gender-specific circumplex fit values, yielding a 24-item version.
Importantly, we used only T1 data to construct the short form and subsequently evaluated the same 24 items at T2, approximately six months later, providing a form of temporal crossvalidation.
We computed available-item domain means and applied the SSM separately to boys and girls at the theoretical RIASEC angles.
The search used 120 ants per iteration, an evaporation parameter of 0.90, and seed 10, and stopped after 60 consecutive iterations without improvement in the best solution.
Each candidate SSM analysis used 100 bootstrap resamples to estimate uncertainty.

text.text: Higher absolute values of PT and DI indicate a stronger orientation along the respective axis.

For PT, positive values indicate a stronger Things-oriented profile (greater relative emphasis on domains located on the Things side of the circumplex, e.g., Realistic), whereas negative values indicate a stronger People-oriented profile (greater emphasis on domains located on the People side, e.g., Social).

For DI, positive values indicate a stronger Ideas-oriented profile (greater emphasis on domains located on the Ideas side, e.g., Artistic), whereas negative values indicate a stronger Data-oriented profile (greater emphasis on domains located on the Data side, e.g., Conventional).
Values close to zero reflect a more balanced profile with little net orientation on that axis.
We used the PT, DI, and PE values as person-related variables to correlate with the covariates of academic interests and school grades.

To evaluate the short-term temporal stability and potential gender-differential change, we estimated linear mixed-effects models with repeated observations nested within children and children clustered in classes (random intercepts for child and class, respectively).

text.text: We first evaluated the fit of the circumplex models using the theoretically developed 42-item RIASEC questionnaire.
Fit was good for girls (R² = .919) but insufficient for boys (R² = .374) at T1.
Given that this was the first empirical application of the questionnaire, we used the data of T1 to inform the construction of a short scale.
Specifically, we applied the metaheuristic ACO to select four items for each RIASEC domain, while simultaneously aiming for satisfactory model fit for both gender groups.
The resulting 24-item version showed higher fit at T1, with R² = .928 for boys and .934 for girls.
Importantly, the same item set was evaluated at T2 without further selection as a kind of temporal cross-validation.
Fit of the circumplex model remained satisfactory at this second measurement occasion, with R² = .888 for boys and .945 for girls (Table 1).

The structural summary parameters for the optimized item set revealed that boys' and girls' profiles differed primarily in their angular location (displacement parameter), whereas amplitude and elevation were broadly similar across gender groups.

That is, at the first measurement point (T1), boys exhibited an angular displacement of 49.35°, which positions their peak interest between the Realistic (0°) and Investigative (60°) domains, closer to Investigative.
In contrast, girls showed an angular displacement of 94.20°, reflecting a peak orientation between the Investigative (60°) and Artistic (120°) domains, closer to Artistic.
Therefore, the main distinction between girls and boys was the location of their respective profile peak within the circumplex space.
In contrast to that, amplitude estimates were of comparable size across gender groups at T1, suggesting no clear difference in the overall degree of profile differentiation.
Lastly, profile elevation was similar for boys (3.64) and girls (3.55), indicating that both groups showed comparable overall levels of interest at T1.

This interpretation is also supported by the respective confidence intervals of the parameters: whereas amplitude and elevation showed considerable overlap across gender groups, the confidence intervals for displacement indicated a clearer separation between groups.

Taken together, these analyses again showed that the gendered organization of interest profiles was already clearly visible in Grade 3 and showed little mean-level change over approximately six months.

As indicated before, on the PT dimension, girls' profiles were more strongly oriented toward people, whereas boys' profiles were more strongly oriented toward things, suggesting an early gender difference in the overall direction of vocational-like interests.
There was no clear evidence that PT orientation changed over the observed six months, neither for boys nor girls.
For the DI dimension, girls' profiles were more strongly on the Ideas side than boys', and this difference became somewhat more pronounced over time.
For the level of interest (PE), the results showed a small general decline over six months and this slight decrease was less pronounced for girls than for boys.

Overall, the findings suggest limited short-term mean-level change in the organization of children's interest profiles, specifically with regard to the gender-related differences on the People-Things and Data-Ideas dimensions.

text.text: To connect activity-based and subject-specific accounts of interest, we developed a RIASEC-based self-report for elementary school children and examined gender-related profiles, change over six months, and associations with academic interests and grades.
The 24-item version selected at T1 showed good circumplex fit for boys and girls at both measurement points.
T2 provided temporal cross-validation of the selected item set.
Children's preferences for concrete activities showed a systematic organization beyond school subjects and clear gender-related differences.
Below, we discuss the measurement results, gender differences, stability, and academic correlates before considering the study's limitations.
Structural analyses of the full item pool yielded better circumplex fit for girls than for boys.
This difference may reflect the activities described by the items and how children interpret them.
For example, the Realistic item "helping with repairs" shares the verb "helping" with Social items such as "helping sick people" and "helping others feel comfortable."
A child may endorse this item because they like repairing things or because they like helping an adult, so it may carry social meaning in addition to its intended Realistic content.

More generally, younger children may group activities by surface features, such as a shared verb or the people involved, and by whether an activity seems typical for boys or girls, and item selection may affect gender differences in assessed interests (Tracey & Caulum, 2015; Tracey & Ward, 1998).

text.text: If such interpretations differ between boys and girls, the resulting pattern of correlations may also differ from the expected circumplex structure.
Another possible explanation concerns the reading demands of the self-report questionnaire.
Given average gender differences in reading achievement during primary school (Mullis et al., 2017), some boys may have found particular item formulations more difficult to understand or interpret.

text.text: Finally, familiarity with the specific activities may also play a role (Borgers et al., 2000).

text.text: However, these explanations remain speculative because we did not assess item comprehension or interpretation.
Another question is whether the selected items adequately cover the six RIASEC domains.
Content coverage refers to how well the items represent the range of activities associated with each domain (Haynes et al., 1995; Sireci, 1998).
text.formatted: Content coverage refers to how well the items represent the range of activities associated with each domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Haynes et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Sireci, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: The original questionnaire was developed with reference to Holland's model and established interest inventories.
The short form retains four of seven items in each domain, leaving some activities underrepresented.

For example, all four retained Investigative items involve experimenting or observing (e.g., conducting experiments in a laboratory, looking through a microscope), whereas the three omitted items concerned studying the behavior of animals or plants, reading newspaper articles about difficult topics, and listening to or watching the news.
Because the universe of relevant activities is broad and cannot be sampled exhaustively, some loss of coverage is unavoidable (Markus & Borsboom, 2013).
text.formatted: Because the universe of relevant activities is broad and cannot be sampled exhaustively, some loss of coverage is unavoidable <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Markus & Borsboom, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Future work should therefore examine the extent to which the circumplex structure depends on the specific item set and how children interpret the described activities.
Beyond content coverage, the short form also needs to be evaluated in terms of its psychometric properties.
Shortening a questionnaire can affect its psychometric properties (Kruyen et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Shortening a questionnaire can affect its psychometric properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kruyen et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Smith et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The 24 items selected at T1 also showed good circumplex fit at T2, approximately six months later.
However, because both assessments involved the same cohort, the short form still needs to be evaluated in an independent sample.

The present study revealed consistent gender differences in the circumplex framework: boys reported higher interests in Realistic and Enterprising, whereas girls reported higher Artistic and Social interests.
On the coordinate level of the RIASEC space, boys were more Things-oriented on the People-Things axis, whereas girls were more Ideasoriented on the Data-Ideas axis.
Effect sizes on the People-Things dimension were substantial (d = 0.77), comparable in magnitude to those reported in adult samples (Su et al., 2009).

text.text: For Data-Ideas, the gender difference was smaller (d = -0.37) but in the same direction as in older cohorts.
These mean differences resemble gender-related preferences documented in older samples (Su et al., 2009).

text.text: The present observational data do not identify mechanisms.
The same pattern could reflect activity opportunities, social feedback, perceived competence, or different interpretations of the items.
It is compatible with accounts in which children use gender-typed meanings to judge which activities fit them (Hannover & Wolter, 2019).
text.formatted: It is compatible with accounts in which children use gender-typed meanings to judge which activities fit them <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hannover & Wolter, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Related findings concern gender stereotypes about intellectual ability at age six (Bian et al., 2017) and associations of adults' gender role attitudes with children's motivation in preschool (Wolter et al., 2015).

text.text: Our findings show gender-related preferences beyond particular school subjects in this third-grade sample.
They do not identify when these differences first arose or show that early interventions would change later participation.
The two-wave design permits an assessment of short-term change and stability over six months.

Generalization also requires studies in other cultural and socioeconomic contexts, given evidence that gender differences in preferences vary between societies (Falk & Hermle, 2018; Stoet & Geary, 2018).

text.text: The mixed-effects models showed little change in the average People-Things gender difference over six months.
Data-Ideas scores increased slightly, somewhat more for girls, and profile elevation declined slightly, more for boys.
These are findings about mean-level change.
Despite relatively small changes in the group-level profiles, the six RIASEC dimensions showed only moderate rank-order stability over six months (manifest rs = .38-.52; latent rs = .51-.64).
Both forms of stability need to be distinguished; an unchanged group mean does not imply that children retain the same relative positions.
The six-month interval is too short to determine whether gender differences increase with age or contribute to later educational and occupational choices.
Longer follow-ups could examine these questions in relation to earlier longitudinal work (Hoff et al., 2018; Morgan et al., 2013; Stoll et al., 2017).

text.text: The correlations between academic interests and RIASEC-based activity preferences were small to moderate.

Interest in a school subject is therefore a weak indicator of a child's broader activity preferences, although it may be the most readily available information when children's educational pathways are discussed.
A child's interest in mathematics or German says little about whether that child prefers building, investigating, helping, or organizing.
When these preferences are relevant to educational guidance or later career counseling, practitioners should assess them directly using measures with age-appropriate item wording.
Moreover, some scales have limited reliability, which can attenuate correlations and reduce the precision of individual profile coordinates.
We also did not test incremental validity, so the present results do not show that activity-based interests predict grades beyond academic interests.

The partial overlap may reflect different experiences: academic interests are closely tied to instruction, and activity preferences may also develop through family routines, hobbies, and extracurricular activities (Bryant et al., 2006).

text.text: Earlier reviews and longitudinal research describe gradual development and differentiation of interests across childhood and adolescence (Gfrörer et al., 2022; Hartung et al., 2005).

text.text: The small and sometimes unspecific associations in our study are consistent with a need to assess both kinds of preferences directly, rather than substituting one for the other.
Several limitations must be taken into account when interpreting the results.
First, the 24-item short form was developed through exploratory item selection using T1 data.
Datadriven item selection can capitalize on chance characteristics of a sample (MacCallum et al., 1992), a concern that has also been raised for ACO-based measure development (Dong & Dumas, 2025).

text.text: Some of the shortened scales also had low reliability, which limits measurement precision.

Second, our reliance on child self-reports introduces its own concerns regarding response styles, reading comprehension, and the cognitive demands of self-assessment at this age (Goecke et al., 2022).

text.text: Third, the six-month interval is too short to draw strong conclusions about the developmental trajectory of interest structures across elementary school; longitudinal followups would be needed to examine whether the circumplex becomes more differentiated across middle childhood and how stability develops into adolescence (Tracey, 2002; Xu & Tracey, 2016).

text.text: Fourth, the recruitment procedure may limit the generalizability of our findings.

Participating schools were recruited through the HCAP, an extracurricular enrichment program for gifted elementary school children, and the mean HISEI of the analytical sample was somewhat higher than in a representative sample of fourth graders in Germany.
Schools with a stronger interest in enrichment programs and families with higher occupational status are therefore overrepresented.
Such selection may bias the results if participation is associated with children's activity preferences.
Thus, the observed profiles and gender differences have to be replicated in a larger representative sample of primary school children.
All schools were located in one German federal state, so generalizability to other educational systems and cultural settings remains to be established.
The independent sample needed to validate the short form should therefore be drawn from a broader range of schools and regions.
Fifth, most questionnaire-level missingness resulted from the planned booklet design, but incomplete item responses (approximately 1%) and attrition at T2 (27.4%) also occurred.

Included and excluded children, as well as T2 respondents and children with T1 data only, differed only slightly in the variables we compared, but differences in variables we did not assess, such as test motivation, cannot be ruled out.
The available-case analyses and sensitivity checks cannot eliminate potential bias due to such unplanned missingness (Schafer & Graham, 2002).
text.formatted: The available-case analyses and sensitivity checks cannot eliminate potential bias due to such unplanned missingness <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Schafer & Graham, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the original item provided only binary girl/boy response options and did not distinguish gender identity from sex assigned at birth.
We therefore cannot separate interest patterns associated with gender identity from those associated with sex assigned at birth.

Future research should examine how specific socialization experiences, instructional contexts, and opportunity structures contribute to the emergence, maintenance, and intensification of gendered interest profiles in both scholastic and vocational interests (Eccles & Wigfield, 2024; Master et al., 2025).

text.text: Ideally, such studies should link interest development to concrete experiences in the family, peer group, and classroom.

The present study suggests that third graders' preferences for concrete activities can be assessed with an age-appropriate self-report instrument and that gender-typed profiles along the People-Things dimension are already visible in middle childhood.
The 24-item version selected at T1 showed good circumplex fit for boys and girls in temporal cross-validation at T2.
Nonetheless, this item selection and dimensional structure should be replicated in an independent sample.
For educational psychology, these findings suggest that interest research in elementary school need not be limited to curricular domains.

For vocational psychology, they indicate that circumplex-based interest models may be examined at younger ages than has typically been done, provided that the measures are validated for this age group.

Integrating these two perspectives may help clarify how early motivational orientations evolve through school-based and out-of-school experiences and how they accumulate into the consequential interest profiles observed in adolescence and adulthood.
In this sense, education may either foster or constrain a gendered pathway of interest development.
